blocks.title: Why Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting matters here

spans.text: Problem statement: A policy bot fails on new refund rules and the team must choose prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning. The learner's job is not to memorize Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting; it is to decide what to build or change, what evidence the system may use, and how to tell whether the change improved new-policy answer accuracy after the smallest viable change.

Running case: adaptation decision tree with examples and costs. We will keep this same case through the lesson so each idea has a job: frame the problem, explain the mechanism, choose a design, test the implementation, and decide what to do next.

Before reading on, predict: if fine-tuning is used to teach facts that should have lived in retrieval, where would you look first - the input, the state or data, the model boundary, the validation check, or the release process?
The lesson keeps concrete objects on the page: a real request, the information the system can see, the decision it makes, the output it returns, and the check that catches a wrong answer.

items.text: Product framing: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting matters when it changes a user-visible decision, release gate, or operational workflow.
Engineering framing: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting matters when it changes data, state, prompts, model behavior, tools, schemas, traces, or runtime constraints.
Validation framing: the lesson is not complete until the team can measure new-policy answer accuracy after the smallest viable change on examples that resemble the real workload.

blocks.title: Fully worked example: adaptation decision tree with examples and costs

spans.text: Scenario: A policy bot fails on new refund rules and the team must choose prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning. The team wants to improve new-policy answer accuracy after the smallest viable change, but it has already seen this failure: fine-tuning is used to teach facts that should have lived in retrieval.
Here is the whole worked artifact in one place. Read it as a complete example, not as disconnected tips.
Complete worked artifact

items.text: Question: "Can I get a refund after 35 days if I lost my invoice?" The answer must cite the exact policy chunk, not a plausible refund rule remembered by the model.

Artifact: adaptation decision tree with examples and costs. It specifies loaders, chunk metadata, retriever settings, prompt contract, citation format, and a faithfulness check for new-policy answer accuracy after the smallest viable change.
Worked output: retrieve policy-refunds-v3 section 4, quote "30 days" and "invoice id required", answer that the request probably fails the policy, and link the source chunk used.

spans.text: Complete AI-assistant prompt for this artifact

Role: RAG reviewer. Context: A policy bot fails on new refund rules and the team must choose prompting, RAG, or fine-tuning. Task: inspect adaptation decision tree with examples and costs. Require a user question, retrieved chunks with source ids, final answer, and a claim-by-claim support check. Constraints: do not allow claims that are absent from retrieved chunks; flag stale or missing metadata. Output: {question, retrieved_sources, answer, unsupported_claims, release_decision}.
Why this is richer than a definition
The example ties Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting to a specific input, output, decision, failure mode, and metric. That is the move you should repeat when applying the lesson to your own system.

blocks.title: Mechanism: the mechanism in the running case

spans.text: Mechanism opens the machinery behind Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting. In the running case, the important question is: what exactly changes between the user's request and the final output?
Mechanism means separating retrieval quality from answer quality: did the system fetch the right evidence, and did the model stay faithful to that evidence?
Two framings for the same idea

items.text: Plain framing: imagine a reviewer following a checklist. They need to see what came in, what was considered, what was rejected, and why the final answer is safe to use.
Technical framing: imagine a trace. It should expose inputs, state, external evidence, model or algorithm output, validation result, and owner for exceptions.

blocks.title: Case study: what changed after the first review

spans.text: The first prototype works on the demo path. Then a reviewer runs the uncomfortable case: fine-tuning is used to teach facts that should have lived in retrieval. The output still looks confident, which is exactly why the lesson needs a richer artifact.

The team does not restart from scratch. It adds one missing control to adaptation decision tree with examples and costs: a stricter input contract, better source metadata, a validation assertion, a human-review edge, a rollback trigger, or an audit log depending on where the failure appeared.

items.text: Decision made: keep the thin slice, but block release until the failure is observable and repeatable.
Evidence added: the artifact now shows the input, intermediate evidence, final output, and pass/fail reason.
Metric promoted: new-policy answer accuracy after the smallest viable change becomes part of the release gate instead of a dashboard someone checks later.

spans.text: Case-study takeaway: a useful Fine-tuning vs RAG vs Prompting design makes the wrong answer inspectable before it reaches users.

blocks.title: How this breaks in practice

spans.text: The failure mode to keep in view is concrete: fine-tuning is used to teach facts that should have lived in retrieval. Use it as a diagnostic lens while reading every design choice.

items.text: Retrieved chunks mention the right keyword but not the answer-bearing paragraph.
The answer is relevant but unfaithful: it adds a policy or fact not present in the retrieved evidence.
Metadata is missing, so citations cannot be checked or reranked later.
The broad warning sign: new-policy answer accuracy after the smallest viable change gets worse even though the final answer or artifact still looks polished.

spans.text: Debugging rule: inspect the earliest place where bad evidence can enter and the latest place where validation should have stopped it.

blocks.avoidWhen: Avoid advanced optimization while the team still cannot reproduce or detect: fine-tuning is used to teach facts that should have lived in retrieval.
blocks.ruleOfThumb: Make the failure visible before making the system more sophisticated.
